title: Cognitive Load and Team Boundaries

know: Cognitive load and its kinds as Team Topologies uses them, and how to assess a team's load.
Fracture planes: the differences in domain, rate of change, risk or technology along which a boundary can be drawn.
believe: An overloaded team is helped by owning less or carrying less, not by more people.
can_do: Assess whether a team owns too much or too little, with stated signals.
Propose where to split a team's scope and say which fracture plane justifies it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a description of a team and its scope, the reader says whether it is overloaded, names the signals, and proposes a split along a fracture plane.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A team of seven owns checkout, the tax engine, fraud rules and the invoicing batch jobs; it has had four incidents this quarter, all in areas only one person understands. What would you do, and why not add two engineers?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Overloaded: single-person knowledge and incidents are the signals; split along domain and risk planes (for example payments risk apart from invoicing); adding people raises coordination without lowering what each must understand.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter states when a boundary should not be drawn although a fracture plane exists.
Cognitive load and fracture plane are defined before use and credited to Team Topologies; bounded context is credited to Evans.

thesis.question: How much can one team own, and where should the boundary between two teams go?
thesis.claim: A team can own only what its members can change and operate without relying on one particular person's knowledge, so ownership is sized by cognitive load — the complexity of the domain plus the mechanics the team must also carry — and a boundary belongs on a fracture plane where the domain, the rate of change or the risk differs, and not where the headcount divides evenly.
thesis.disputed_by: The practice of sizing teams by budget and assigning scope by the current backlog, on the assumption that capable engineers can own whatever they are given.
thesis.so_what: An overloaded team is relieved by removing scope or by moving mechanics to a platform, and a request for headcount is tested first against what the team already has to understand.
thesis.how_why: Attention is the first scarce capacity: beyond a certain load a team stops understanding parts of what it owns, and those parts are changed slowly, by one person, or not at all. Two areas that use different domain language, change at different rates or carry different risk need little shared knowledge to cooperate, so the interface between them can stay narrow; a cut through an area that changes together forces both sides to understand both halves.

supporting_claims.claim: A team owns a thing only when its members can change and operate it without relying on one particular person, and cognitive load — the complexity of the domain plus the mechanics the team must also carry — limits how much it can own in that sense.
Whether a team owns too much or too little can be assessed from stated signals: single-person knowledge, rising lead time for the team's other work, areas nobody changes, and the team's own answer.
An overloaded team is relieved by removing scope or by moving mechanics to a platform; adding people leaves what each member must understand unchanged and raises coordination.

A boundary belongs on a fracture plane, where the domain, the rate of change or the risk differs, because areas that differ in those ways need little shared knowledge to cooperate; a cut by headcount runs through areas that change together.
A fracture plane permits a boundary and does not require one: the cut is not made when most changes would cross it, when a resulting team could not operate its part, or when nobody's load would fall.

role.contribution: Gives the sizing rule for a component and the rule for placing boundaries, which Part II turns into team types and sizes.

additional_patterns.applies_to: cognitive-load before assess-the-load and relieve-the-load; fracture-planes before test-the-cut: each supplies the terms the next uses

flow.rationale: The scene shows two decisions that used headcount as the measure and leaves two questions, how much and where. The chapter answers them in that order because the second arises from the first: the remedy for too much is to remove scope, and removing scope requires a place to cut. Within each answer the concept comes before the pattern that uses it. If fracture planes came first the reader would learn where to cut before knowing why any cut was needed, and the planes' justification, which rests on what each side must understand, would have no term to rest on. The anti-patterns follow both answers because each misuses one of them, the worked example uses every term and closes the 2023 cut on which the scene ended, and the AI section is a coda after it.

hook.content: Late in 2022 the manager of Corvane's Core team asked for two more engineers. Core had six, and earlier that year it had taken on the rule engine on top of the shared services it already ran. The request was granted. A quarter after the two engineers joined, Core's lead time for its other work was a day longer than before.

bridge.from_reader_world: Most readers have approved or asked for headcount for a struggling team and seen the team struggle on.
bridge.to_topic: If more people did not help, the shortage was not of people; it was of what the team could understand, and that has its own sizing rule and its own rule for where to cut.

thesis_statement.text: A team can own only what its members can change and operate without relying on one particular person. Ownership is therefore sized by cognitive load, the complexity of the domain plus the mechanics the team must also carry, and a boundary belongs on a fracture plane, where the domain, the rate of change or the risk differs, and not where the headcount divides evenly.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

promises.promise: See a team given more people for a problem of scope, and a company cut into teams by headcount.
Define cognitive load and its three kinds, and the test for what a team owns.
Assess whether a team owns too much or too little from stated signals.
Relieve an overloaded team by removing scope or mechanics, and see why people do not relieve it.
Define fracture planes and place a boundary on one.
Test a cut before making it, and know when not to make it.
Recognize the usual ways sizing and cutting go wrong.
Follow Corvane re-cutting two of its teams, and see what AI changes about the sizing rule.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane's Core team asked for two more engineers after taking on the rule engine, got them, and was no faster a quarter later.

evidence.what: Corvane, late 2022, about 45 engineers: Core has six engineers and owns the rule engine since the 2022 fix on top of its shared services; its manager asks for two engineers; they join in January 2023; a quarter later Core's median lead time for work outside the rule engine is 12 days, against 11 before they joined.
evidence.shows: A remedy sized in people did not relieve a team whose problem was what it had to understand.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What a team can own is sized by cognitive load and not by headcount, and a boundary between two teams belongs on a fracture plane; the chapter takes the two questions in that order.

transition_in.carries_over: A team that got more people and did not get faster.
transition_in.introduces: The sizing rule and the placing rule that explain it, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: Six Engineers and a Request for Two More
sections.controlling_idea: Twice in two years Corvane used headcount as the measure of what a team could own, once to relieve a team and once to cut eleven, and both times the measure missed what the teams had to understand.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the two cases the chapter explains: people added to an overloaded team, and a boundary placed by dividing people evenly.

flow.rationale: The request, the remedy and the later cut are told in the order they happened so the reader sees the same assumption applied twice.

transition_in.carries_over: The lead's short account of the request for two engineers.
transition_in.introduces: What Core owned, what was observed, and what Corvane did next.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In late 2022 Core, six engineers, owned three shared services and their deployment scripts, and since that year's fix the rule engine as well.

evidence.what: Corvane, the fictional company this book follows, late 2022, about 45 engineers at the start of its hiring wave. Core owns accounts and sign-in, notification delivery, the shared data model for customers and jobs, its own deployment scripts, and the rule engine for scheduling and job-status rules that the 2022 fix moved into it.
evidence.shows: Sets out the scope that six people were asked to own.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The signs were that one engineer alone could change part of the rule engine and that Core's lead time for everything else had nearly tripled.

evidence.what: Samir Haddad, a staff engineer, was the only person who could safely change the rule engine's overlap logic (whether two jobs for one technician conflict); Core's median lead time for work outside the rule engine rose from 4 days to 11.
evidence.shows: The two observations the manager's request rested on.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.introduces: What that scope did to the team's work.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane gave Core two more engineers, and a quarter later the lead time was 12 days, because the new engineers had to learn the scope from the person who was already the constraint.

evidence.what: Two engineers joined Core in January 2023; a quarter later the median lead time for other work was 12 days; Samir Haddad spent much of that quarter explaining the rule engine.
evidence.shows: More people did not reduce what had to be understood, and used up the one person who understood it.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.introduces: The remedy chosen and its result.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2023 Corvane cut itself into eleven product teams by dividing people evenly; Core's shared services went to new teams, and the cut ran through the middle of the rule engine.

evidence.what: 2023: eleven product teams of about eight. Core was dissolved: accounts and sign-in went to Identity, notification delivery to Notifications, the shared data model and the deployment scripts to the platform team formed in 2022. The rule engine was divided: Scheduling got the scheduling rules, the planner calendar screens and travel-time estimation (a separate service built on map data and a routing library); Dispatch got the job-status rules and the live dispatch board. In the first half of 2024, 23 of 31 rule changes needed both teams.
evidence.shows: A line placed by headcount separated two things that changed together.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.introduces: The reorganization of 2023 and where its lines fell.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Both decisions measured ownership in people, and neither asked what a team would have to understand, which leaves two questions: how much one team can own, and where the line between two teams should go.

transition_in.introduces: What they have in common and the two questions they leave open.

sections.heading: Cognitive Load: What One Team Can Hold
sections.controlling_idea: What a team can own is limited by its cognitive load, the mental effort of understanding the domain plus the mechanics it carries, and the test of ownership is that the team can change and operate a thing without relying on one particular person.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the sizing rule: the term, its kinds, the ownership test and the limit of the concept.

flow.rationale: The term is defined before its kinds, the kinds before the ownership test, which applies to the sum of the first two kinds, and the test before the account of what happens when a team fails it; the rule of thumb and the limit of the concept come last because they qualify a rule the reader must already hold, and placed earlier they would qualify a term not yet defined.

transition_in.carries_over: The first open question: how much one team can own.
transition_in.introduces: The concept that answers it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Cognitive load, as Team Topologies uses the term, is the total mental effort a team needs to understand, change and operate what it owns; the book treats it as the thing to restrict when sizing a team's responsibilities, and in this book's terms it is how the scarce capacity of attention shows up for one team.

evidence.what: Skelton and Pais argue for putting the team first and restricting its cognitive load, and say that thinking explicitly about cognitive load is a tool for deciding team size, assigning responsibilities and setting boundaries with other teams. The term comes from John Sweller's research on learning; Sweller is cited only for the origin and supplements the author's sources.
evidence.shows: Credits the concept to its source and states what it is used for.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Team Topologies distinguishes three kinds of load — intrinsic, extraneous and germane — and this book reads them as the complexity of the domain, the mechanics the team must also carry, and the learning that makes the team better at its domain.

evidence.what: Kind | What it is | At Core in 2022 | What to do with it. Intrinsic | the complexity of the domain itself | the scheduling and job-status rules | accept it and size the scope to it. Extraneous | mechanics around the work: release steps, tooling, process, hand-offs | Core's own deployment scripts | remove it or move it to a platform. Germane | learning the domain and solving its problems | understanding why planners double-book | protect it.
evidence.shows: Separates the load that must be carried from the load that can be removed.
evidence.source: Team Topologies (2019), as summarized in the author's records team-first-thinking and team-first-boundaries and the Team-First checklists

transition_in.introduces: Its three kinds and what to do with each.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team owns a thing only when its members can change it and operate it without relying on one particular person.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: every part of the system is owned by exactly one team, with no shared ownership.
evidence.shows: Ownership belongs to a team; the test says when a team really has it.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

evidence.what: A thing only one person can change is owned by that person and not by the team: it cannot be changed when that person is away and is not operated by the people on call.
evidence.shows: Turns the limit into a test a reader can apply.

transition_in.carries_over: Load as domain complexity plus mechanics, with a limit.
transition_in.introduces: The test of ownership that follows from the limit.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Past its limit a team stops understanding parts of what it owns, and those parts are changed slowly, by one person, or not at all.

evidence.what: "If we stress the team by giving it responsibility for part of the system that is beyond its cognitive load capacity, it ceases to act like a high-performing unit and starts to behave like a loosely associated group of individuals, each trying to accomplish their individual tasks without the space to consider if those are in the team's best interest."
evidence.shows: The source's account of overload: the team dissolves into individuals, which is what single-person knowledge looks like from outside.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

transition_in.introduces: What happens when a team is given more than passes it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Team Topologies offers a rule of thumb for how much is too much: classify each domain as simple, complicated or complex, and give a team at most one complex domain and not several complicated ones.

evidence.what: The authors' heuristic, as the author's Team-First Thinking checklist records it: classify domains as simple, complicated or complex; do not assign a complex domain plus additional domains to one team; avoid giving one team several complicated domains.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader a first sizing rule, presented as the source's rule of thumb and not as a law.
evidence.source: Team Topologies (2019), as summarized in the author's records team-first-thinking and team-first-boundaries and the Team-First checklists

transition_in.introduces: A rule of thumb for staying short of it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Cognitive load cannot be measured, only assessed: the source's own method is to ask the team, and applying a concept from individual learning to a whole team is a working idea and not an established measure.

evidence.what: "A simple and quick way to assess cognitive load is to ask the team, in a non-judgmental way: 'Do you feel like you're effective and able to respond in a timely fashion to the work you are asked to do?'"
evidence.shows: The source itself offers a question, not a metric.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

transition_in.carries_over: A rule of thumb that sounds like a calculation.
transition_in.introduces: The limit: there is no number, and where the evidence runs out.

sections.heading: Pattern: Assess a Team's Load from What It Owns
sections.controlling_idea: A team's load is assessed by listing what it owns, asking of each area who can change it and who can operate it, and reading four signals of too much and three of too little.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the ownership test into a procedure with stated signals, for overload and for underload.

flow.rationale: The procedure comes first because the signals are read from the list it produces; the signals come before Core's list so the reader can read that list without help, and the list comes before its reading so the example is shown before it is judged; underload comes last because it is read from the same list by the opposite signs, and placed first it would describe the rarer case before the common one.

transition_in.carries_over: A load that can only be assessed.
transition_in.introduces: A way to assess it that does not depend on opinion alone.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The assessment is an ownership list with a count: for each area the team owns, how many members can change it safely and how many can operate it; its user is the team's lead and the leader who assigns its scope, and its outcome measure is the number of areas where either count is below two.

evidence.what: The author's procedure, built on the ownership test: an area with a count of one is owned by a person; a count of zero is owned by nobody.
evidence.shows: Makes the assessment repeatable and gives it a number that can be tracked over quarters.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four signals say that a team owns too much.

evidence.what: Signal | What you see | What it tells you. Single-person knowledge | an area only one member can change or operate | the team does not own it; the person does. Lead time rising for the team's other work | older areas wait while the newest takes the attention | scope was added without anything being removed. Areas nobody changes | requests in one area are postponed or worked around | the team has stopped understanding it. The team's own answer | the team says it cannot respond in time | the source's direct question, answered.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader named signals to quote in an assessment; the list is the author's, built on Team Topologies.
evidence.source: Team Topologies (2019), as summarized in the author's records team-first-thinking and team-first-boundaries and the Team-First checklists

transition_in.introduces: The signals that go with it, and what each one means.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ownership list for Core in late 2022 has five areas, each with its kind and its two counts.

evidence.what: Area | Kind | Can change it | Can operate it. Rule engine | complex | 1 (overlap logic), 3 (the rest) | 3. Accounts and sign-in | complicated | 2 | 4. Notification delivery | complicated | 3 | 4. Shared data model | complicated | 2 | 3. Deployment scripts | mechanics | 1 | 2.
evidence.shows: The raw list, shown before it is judged.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.introduces: The signals read off one team.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Core's list shows one complex domain, three complicated ones and a set of mechanics, with two areas that one person alone could change, so Core broke the rule of thumb and failed the ownership test twice.

transition_in.introduces: What it shows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team can also own too little, and the signs are the reverse: most of its changes need another team, it cannot staff its own on-call rotation, or it fills its time with work nobody asked for.

evidence.what: The author's experience, marked as such: Team Topologies' checklists warn about overload; the three signs of underload are not from the source.
evidence.shows: Completes the assessment in the other direction and labels the evidence honestly.

transition_in.introduces: Too little, by the opposite signs.

sections.heading: Pattern: Relieve the Load by Removing Scope or Mechanics
sections.controlling_idea: An overloaded team is relieved by owning less or carrying less, and a request for headcount is first tested against what the new people would have to understand.

advances_thesis.how: Argues the chapter's belief: people do not relieve overload, removing scope or mechanics does, and states when adding people is right.

flow.rationale: Why the obvious remedy fails comes first, so that the pattern arrives as the alternative; the comparison of the three remedies follows the pattern, and the caveat about platforms comes last because it qualifies one of the remedies.

transition_in.introduces: What relieves it, starting with why the usual remedy does not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adding people to an overloaded team does not lower what each member must understand, and it adds teaching and coordination to the people who are already the constraint.

evidence.what: Scope is not divided by headcount: on call, in review and in design each member still meets the whole of it. New members learn from those who know, as Core's two engineers did from Samir Haddad.
evidence.shows: Explains Core's result from the scene.

evidence.what: Team Topologies treats a team as small, about five to nine people by the authors' rule of thumb, so a team cannot grow its way out of a scope that is too large.
evidence.shows: A second reason: growth has a ceiling.
evidence.source: Team Topologies (2019), as summarized in the author's records team-first-thinking and team-first-boundaries and the Team-First checklists

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern is to take something away: move a domain to another team, or move mechanics to a platform; its user is the overloaded team, and its outcome measures are the count of single-person areas and the lead time for the team's other work.

transition_in.carries_over: A remedy that does not work.
transition_in.introduces: The two that do, with user and measure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three remedies change different things, and adding people is the right one only when the team understands all it owns and has more work than hands.

evidence.what: Remedy | What it changes | What it costs | Right when. Remove scope | what the team must understand | a new boundary and an interface to own | the team holds a complex domain plus others, or unrelated domains. Move mechanics to a platform | what the team must carry besides its domain | a dependency on the platform | the load is release steps, tooling or infrastructure that several teams repeat. Add people | hands, not understanding | onboarding, more coordination | every area passes the ownership test and the work still exceeds the team.
evidence.shows: Makes the choice a decision with conditions and concedes the case for hiring.

transition_in.carries_over: Two remedies recommended and one rejected.
transition_in.introduces: What each changes, what it costs and when it fits.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Moving mechanics to a platform relieves a team only when the platform is self-service; otherwise the team exchanges load for a queue, as Corvane found in 2024.

evidence.what: Corvane formed a platform team in 2022, and Core's deployment scripts went to it in 2023. 2024, 180 people: five platform engineers for eleven product teams, 14 open launch requests at the peak, lead time for a change 19 days.
evidence.shows: The same move that lowers a team's load can create a wait, which the next chapter takes up.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.introduces: The condition under which it is one.

sections.heading: Fracture Planes: Where a Boundary Can Go
sections.controlling_idea: A boundary belongs on a fracture plane, a seam where the domain, the rate of change or the risk differs (technology is a fourth and weaker plane), because two areas that differ in those ways need little shared knowledge and the interface between them can stay narrow.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the placing rule, gives its reasoning, and contrasts it with Corvane's cut by headcount.

flow.rationale: The definition comes before the reasoning, the reasoning before the first plane and its origin in bounded contexts, the four planes together after one has been understood, and the headcount cut last so the reader can judge it with the planes in hand.

transition_in.carries_over: Removing scope means cutting it somewhere, the second open question.
transition_in.introduces: The rule for where.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Removing scope means cutting it somewhere, and Team Topologies names the place: a fracture plane, a natural seam along which a system can be split easily, which this chapter applies to the scope a team owns.

evidence.what: "A fracture plane is a natural seam in the software system that allows the system to be split easily into two or more parts."
evidence.shows: Credits the term and gives its definition before use.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A seam is natural where the two sides need little knowledge of each other, so that the interface between them stays narrow and each side's load stays low; a cut through an area that changes together forces both sides to understand both halves.

transition_in.introduces: Why some lines split easily and others do not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first plane to look for is the business domain, and Evans's bounded context names it: the part of the business within which one model and one vocabulary apply.

evidence.what: Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design (2003): a bounded context is the boundary within which a particular domain model, and the language that goes with it, applies consistently. Cited as the widely known concept; it supplements the author's sources. Team Topologies puts the bounded context first among its fracture planes.
evidence.shows: Credits the concept and gives the reader a test: the same word meaning different things marks the line.
evidence.source: Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design (2003); Team Topologies (2019), as summarized in the author's records team-first-thinking and team-first-boundaries and the Team-First checklists

transition_in.introduces: The strongest kind, with its source.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four planes do most of the work: domain, rate of change, risk and technology, and technology is the weakest.

evidence.what: Plane | What differs | Question to ask | At Corvane. Domain | vocabulary, model and rules | do the two sides use the same words for the same things? | scheduling rules and billing exports. Rate of change | how often each side changes | does one side wait for the other's pace? | planner screens several times a week; each rule change waits for a weekly review. Risk | what an error costs | would a mistake on one side be contained? | a wrong rule alters every customer's schedule. Technology | skills and tools | is the difference a real constraint? | the technicians' mobile app and the office web application. Team Topologies also lists regulatory compliance, performance isolation, team location and user personas.
evidence.shows: Gives each plane a question a reader can ask of a real scope.
evidence.source: Team Topologies (2019), as summarized in the author's records team-first-thinking and team-first-boundaries and the Team-First checklists

transition_in.introduces: The four the chapter uses, each with its question.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Headcount is not a plane: Corvane's 2023 cut put half of the rule engine in each of two teams, and most rule changes then needed both.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart: Scheduling (scheduling rules, planner calendar, travel-time estimation) and Dispatch (job-status rules, live dispatch board), with an edge between the two rule sets labelled '23 of 31 rule changes need both teams'.
evidence.shows: Shows the boundary running through one domain.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: Lines placed where the work differs.
transition_in.introduces: A line placed where the people divided evenly.

sections.heading: Pattern: Test a Cut, and Know When Not to Make It
sections.controlling_idea: A proposed boundary is tested against the record of past changes before it is made, and it is not made, even on a real fracture plane, when most changes would cross it, when a resulting team could not operate its part, when nobody's load would fall, or when the two sides would stay coupled underneath.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the test for a cut and the conditions under which a fracture plane is not enough.

transition_in.carries_over: Planes on which a boundary can go.
transition_in.introduces: How to check a particular boundary before making it, and when to leave it undrawn.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The test is to take the last quarter's changes and count how many would have needed both sides of the proposed line; its user is the two teams the line would create and the teams that depend on them, and its outcome measure is that share, before and after.

evidence.what: "Does the resulting architecture support more autonomous teams (less dependent teams) with reduced cognitive load (less disparate responsibilities)?"
evidence.shows: The source's own question for a proposed split; the count from history is the author's way of answering it with a number.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every boundary replaces shared understanding with an interface that someone has to own, so a cut is worth making only when the load it removes is larger than the interface it adds.

evidence.what: From the chapter on the organization as a system: an interface is a lever only when it has an owner; an unowned one is a failure pattern.
evidence.shows: Ties the limit on cutting to a cost the reader already knows.

transition_in.carries_over: A cut that passes the test.
transition_in.introduces: What every cut costs, even one that passes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A fracture plane therefore says where a boundary may go, not that it must, and there are four cases in which the boundary should not be drawn.

evidence.what: Four cases, as a list: most changes would cross the line; a resulting team would be too small or lack the skills to run and be on call for its part; no team is overloaded, so the cut buys nothing; the two sides would still share a database, a build or a release, which Team Topologies calls hidden monoliths.
evidence.shows: States the conditions the acceptance criteria ask for.
evidence.source: Team Topologies (2019), as summarized in the author's records team-first-thinking and team-first-boundaries and the Team-First checklists

transition_in.introduces: The four cases in which the cost is not repaid, even on a real plane.

flow.rationale: The test comes first because it supplies the count the later paragraphs use; the cost of a boundary comes before the four cases so that they read as instances of one rule and not as a list explained afterwards.

sections.heading: Anti-Patterns: The Capable Team and the Even Split
sections.controlling_idea: Sizing and cutting fail in three recognizable ways: scope is added to a team because it copes, lines are drawn by budget and backlog, and the one person who knows everything is treated as a strength.

advances_thesis.how: Names the failures the sizing rule and the placing rule prevent, and answers the view the thesis disputes.

transition_in.introduces: What is commonly done instead.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Overloaded Team is made by a compliment: scope is given to the team that copes, on the assumption that capable engineers can own whatever they are given.

evidence.what: Capability raises how fast a team learns a domain; it does not remove the limit on how many domains its members can hold at once. Core was given the rule engine in 2022 because it was Corvane's most capable team.
evidence.shows: Answers the view the thesis disputes with the case from the scene.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Org Chart as Architecture, in this chapter's form, is the even split: the budget sets the size of the teams and the current backlog sets their scope.

evidence.what: A backlog describes the next two quarters; a domain outlasts them. Teams drawn around the backlog of 2023 own whatever that backlog happened to contain. Layer teams, one per technology, are the same error with a different divider.
evidence.shows: Explains why Corvane's 2023 cut fell where it did.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Re-Cutting Scheduling and Dispatch
sections.controlling_idea: In 2025 Corvane assessed its Scheduling and Dispatch teams, moved one boundary onto a fracture plane, removed scope from one team and left one possible boundary undrawn, and the share of rule changes that needed two teams fell without any added headcount.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the assessment, the planes and the test, including a boundary not drawn, to the case the scene opened.

flow.rationale: Assessment, decisions, the new boundary and the result are given in the order they happened; the table of findings comes before any judgement of them, and the result comes last so the section ends on what the change achieved and what it cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2025 Dario Vance, Corvane's VP Engineering, asked Samir Haddad to run the assessment on Scheduling and Dispatch, the two teams of eight that shared the rule engine.

Job-status rules move to Scheduling, which owns the whole rule engine | domain: one vocabulary, changing together | share of rule changes needing two teams. sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: Coding agents lower the effort of writing a change in an unfamiliar area and leave the ownership test as it is, and whether they let a team own more is not yet known.

advances_thesis.how: Tests the sizing rule against AI with labeled claims and defers the evidence to Part XI.

transition_in.carries_over: A sizing rule shown at work in 2025.
transition_in.introduces: Whether the rule holds when agents write part of the code.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Emerging: agents make it cheaper to produce a change in code a team does not know well, but the team still has to understand what it owns well enough to review the change, operate it and answer for it, so the ownership test is unchanged.

evidence.what: The author's observation as of November 2026, labeled Emerging, not a measured result; the paragraph opens by announcing the book's three AI labels.
evidence.shows: Places agents against the ownership test with the basis stated.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Speculative: agents may pull a team's load in two directions, down by explaining unfamiliar code and absorbing mechanics, and up by producing more change than the team can understand, and which pull is stronger would show in the count of single-person areas as scope grows.

evidence.what: Labeled Speculative; the evidence is weighed in the chapters Where the Constraint Moves and Team Shape and Roles with AI.
evidence.shows: Marks the claim as reasoning and says what would confirm it.

transition_in.introduces: What may change about how much passes it, and what would confirm it.

flow.rationale: The observation about what agents do today comes before the reasoning about what may follow, because the speculative claim is about a change to the test the first paragraph says is unchanged.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The sizing rule and the placing rule are one rule seen from two sides: a team's scope is right when the team passes the ownership test, and a boundary is right when it lets the teams on both sides pass it with a narrow interface between them; headcount enters only after both are settled.
conclusion.so_what: A leader who receives a request for headcount, or a proposal for a reorganization, can ask first what the team would have to understand and what share of changes would cross the proposed lines, and can decline both people and boundaries that the answers do not support.

callback.to: Core's request for two more engineers in late 2022.
callback.how: The reader can now say what the request left out: two areas only one person could change, a complex domain added on top of three complicated ones, and nothing taken away.

takeaway.content: Take one team that has asked for people, write its ownership list with the two counts, and decide what to remove before deciding whom to hire. The checklist gives the steps.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: a team has a limit on what it can understand, exceeding it turns the team into individuals, every part of a system needs exactly one owning team, and systems split most easily along natural seams, the business domain first.

Depends on context: which remedy fits an overloaded team, which plane to cut on, and whether to cut at all depend on what the load consists of, on how the changes fall and on whether the resulting teams can operate what they get.
